From ike Observer, January 29, 1854. THE EMPEROR NICHOLAS AS A WARRIOR.

People may remember tint Nicholas, when at Varna, prudently kept his steamer out. of the reach of the Turkish guns. Marshal Diebitch undertook the command on condition that neither the Czar nor his brother should remain in Turkey. Since then Nicholas has yielded to the conviction that lie is not able to conduct s» war, and so lie has contented himself with commanding at reviews, tind this he does with delipht and fanaticism. He identifies himself with such manoeuvres so well that he takes them for actual engagements. He takes off his helmet at once, and cries out, "Boys, God for us; into the þÿfire! 40 Another time he gives his aide-de-camp an order to carry, and, forgetting that there was no danger, he says, þÿ Fight , your way through, care not for your family, I will provide for þÿthem. Obliged to surrender Petersburg, he put this clause in the capitulation, that þÿ The winter palace and the Imperial family shall he preserved; if not, he will fight to the last drop of blood þÿ! lie is never victorious, but always beaten. Last year he was surrounded by General Rudiger, and a division marched to cut off from him the last hamlet for his retreat. An aide-de-camp, and afterwards the Minister of War himself, came to the commander of this division, to persuade him hot to perform this manoeuvre; but he says, in reply, shat he must obey his immediate chief. Then they address the same prayer to General Rudiger. þÿ I should like to save his þÿMajesty, answered the old warrior, þÿ but how is

it to he managed? Now, my weakest point is litre ; let the Emperor attack it þÿ let him kill my artillery men, and break through; I will do nothing to prevent þÿit. It happened as he advised, and the Czar, full of joy, said, þÿ Are not my riflemen a splendid idea þÿ? At night he gives orders that the alarm shall not be sounded before eight þÿo clock reports every hour. He wraps himself in the morning, yet to send him | up in his cloak and slumbers. The general who has to send the reports lias them all in readiness and goes to bed, ordering a paper to be taken every hour from his table and carried to the Emperor. Once the Czar killed a great many horses in searching for the enemy, whom he could not meet with, lie ealled the commander of the detachment, and said to him, þÿ Why did I not see you þÿ were you þÿafraid? þÿ have I neither cavalry nor artillery. I must keep in the þÿforest, answered the general. The Czar arrested him, and the general who succeeded him, in order to avoid the same fate, drove the division before the eyes of the Czar, suffered himself to be beaten, but escaped the anger of his Majesty. And such an Emperor is to conquer the world ! One evening, in the þÿEmpress draw- s ing-room, Nicholas opened her album, and stood looking at a drawing, lost in thought. His wife ventured to inquire as to the subject of his thoughts. The subject of the drawing was Godefroy de Bouillon at Jerusalem. þÿ I like such an enterprise, said the þÿCzar, þÿ under- I stand the nature of so great a design.
Yes, go to war for the sake of an idea, to fire the nations of the world with enthusiastic ardour for it þÿ that would please þÿme.
Which is the stronger, lie or truth ? Truth, for you may rc-ly on it.

OB SERVER OFFICE, Saturday Night. LATEST INTELLIGENCE. TELEGRAPHIC DESPATCHES. Varna, Jan. 29. þÿ Omar Pasha is entirely restored to health. A Wallachian general, two or three American officers, and several French and Swedish officers, have arrived to take service in the Ottoman army. Gai.atz, Feb. 2. þÿ The Turks made reconnoitring expeditions from Matschin and Isatchka with steamers and gunboats against Ibraila and Rcni. A sharp firing ensued on both sides. The Turks, having succeeded in their object, ultimately retired. Belgrade, Feb. 3. þÿ A serious fight took place at Tojana on the 29th ult., which was attended with great loss on both sides. The Turks retreated to Kalnfat. Giurgevo, Feb. 6. þÿ On the 5th a smart affair took place near Giurgevo between the Turks and Russians. The loss on either side was considerable. It appears that 3,000 Turks crossed the Danube, routed the Russian outposts, and attacked the town, after which they retired. Bucharest, Feb. 7. þÿ Almost daily attempts have been made by the Turks to cross the Danubo at Giurgevo and Oltenitza since the 15th ult., hut without success. Krajova, Feb. 8. þÿ The had weather has alono prevented the Russians from attacking Kalafat. The investing army has made a movement in advance, hut active operations will not begin before March, when the bridges for crossing the Danube will be ready. Constantinople, Jan. 29. þÿ Considerable reinforcements arc on march from Sophia for Kalafat, whero there is already assembled an army of 25,000 men, provided with a numerous and ex-

cellent train of artillery. The French steam corvette Prometheus returned to-day from Varna, upon which Admiral Hamelin immediately called together a oouncil of his captains, a step which was also taken by Admiral Dundas. The result of this council was that all the larger steamers of both fleets were ordered to convoy a number of Turkish transports, which were first to carry reinforcements to Varna, and thence to proceed to Batoum This convoy was to leave on the 28th.

Constantinople, Jan. 30. þÿ One English and one French steamer have started on a cruise ia the Black Sea. The fortifications of Kalafat are mounted with about 130 heavy pieces of ordnance. Sixteen or eighteen pieces of artillery, of heavy calibre, have lately been transported to Kalafat from the walls of Widdin. Vienna, Feb. 11. þÿ The conference met once more on Friday, the 3rd inst., for the purpose of taking into consideration the answer of the Cabinet of St. Petersburg to the peace project forwarded hence to that city on the 13th ult. The following protocol was drawn up on this occasion : þÿ þÿ The Four Powers declare that the tenor of the said answer of the Russian Cabinet is highly unsatisfactory, and by no means adapted for transmission to the Sublime þÿPorte. THE DANUBE. It is believed that a sanguinary engagement took place at Giurgevo on Sunday, the 5th inst., in which both sides suffered severe loss. The Turks, it is said, crossed the Danube in number three thousand, drove in the outposts, and attempted to take the town. In the end they withdrew across the Danube. A Turkish detachment having passed the Danube in the night, destroyed the tele de pant of the Sercth, between Galatz and Ibraila, which was defended by two thousand Russians. The combat was fierce, and the Russians, who were inferior in numbers, were compelled to abandon the position. The Turks destroyed the þÿenemy large s new barracks. The last-arrived number of the new Russian newspaper published at Bucharest, and entitled

the Wallachian Moniteur, contains a general order by Prince Gortschakoff, enacting: That all the male population from eighteen to forty years of age, married or unmarried, and of whatever profession, may he required by the generals, colonels, or chefs de corps, to render compulsory service robota to the Russian army. That horses, oxen, and all other draught cattle., beside waggons, may in like manner he taken for the same use ; and, lastly, that all the barks, boats, and barges found on the Danube may be taken at any moment for the Russian service. This ordinance applies to all Wallachian subjects, and any person attempting to evade it will he brought before a court martial.

At a late hour on Saturday afternoon Baron Brunow had an interview with the Earl of Clarendon at the Foreign Office, for the purpose of formally suspending the diplomatic relations Go- of the Emperor of Russia with her þÿMajesty s vernment. The Russian Minister withdraws from this country with all the members of the Legation, who are to repair, we believe, to diflerent towns in Germany ; the Russian Consul- General will, however, remain for the present to transact the commercial business of his office. The public arc doubtless aware that a Minister from a Foreign State who is recalled under circumstances like the present is not entitled to the audience of the Queen at which envoys commonly take leave of her Majesty at the termination of their missions. Nevertheless, the recall of an envoy does not constitute a declaration of war , and it must he followed by more decided measures on the one side or the other before a state of war can he said to exist between the two empires The first measure taken by the British Government on the eve of a rupture with a foreign Power has commonly been to stop by Order in Council vessels clearing out from British ports for the ports of the hostile Power ; hut the present state of our relations with Russia has long been so web known to the public that we arc informed no ves sels are clearing out of our ports for that country, and the trado is virtually suspended. Baron Brunow did not leave London till Monday, nor did M. Kissclcff take his departure from
Paris till Monday. The resignation of their diplomatic functions by ambassadors is not any more than their actual departure would he, either for-

such retirement is usually tie: preliminary raally or practically a declaration of war, ot though such a declaration. The practical declaration is generally an embargo upon shipping, or other means of transit. The formal declaration speaks for itself.

We have this week to record one of the most dreadful shipwrecks which has ever perhaps occurred within our recollection. 1 he layleur sailed from the Mersey on Thursday week, having on board about 600 souls, including crew and passengers, of all ages. The ship was towed as tar as Point Lynas, by the steam-tug Victory, and had fair weather for some hours, until she got off struggled Holyhead, when the wind headed her, the and entire aguiust an adverse gale during she of Friday and Friday night. The captain, despairing of getting down the Channel north a gale, determined to try the course against such about Accordingly, the þÿship head s was got round, and she stood on amidst thick and heavy weather from j daylight on Saturday morning. Owing to the dense fog, and, perhaps, to some error in the : reckoning, the ship was found, at about ten þÿo clock, man within at sight of land, which was first seen by the the wheel, and in half-an-hour after the j j look-out man at the bows cried, þÿ Breakers on the starboard þÿbow. The þÿship s course was altered, and in loss than twenty minutes after she struck with fearful violence on a reef of rocks, on the east side of Lambay Island. The terrible consequences of this catastrophe will be best gathered from the subjoined accounts, furnished by some of the passengers In short, out of the entire number on board the ill-fated vessel, (six hundred and sixty, including the crew,) only two hundred and eighty-three individuals have been rescued, and rnauy of these are severely maimed

aud injured. A portion of the passengers and crew, with the captain, effected their escape from the wreck, and got on Lambay Island, where for some time they experienced the extremes of cold and hardship, until relieved and subsequently taken off the island and brought to Dublin. The position and state of the wreck having been correctly reported at the office of þÿLloyd a s gent, the steamer Prince was despatched to Lambay Island, where she stopped her engines and lay-to, | about nightfall on Sunday evening. Captain Dearl, after a consultation with the gentlemen on board, decided to lower the boats and proceed to the island, in order to ascertain how many survivors were vet left on shore, and adopt measures for getting them on board the Prince and convey- \ ing them to Dublin. Accordingly, tlirco boats J were lowered and manned for the purpose. The night was wild and threatening. Mr. Allen, Mr. Brown, and the other gentlemen who went in the boats, accompanied by a portion of the crews, after landing and drawing their craft above highwater m irk, proceeded across the island (about one mile and a half) to the creek where the wrecked vessel lay. The stem and bowsprit were above water, but her decks, amidships, and stern submerged, while the waves were breaking over her masts and rigging. The foremast, foretopmast, and stump of the foretopgallant mast were still standing ; the main and mizon topmast had | been carried away ; the foretopsail remained still set, hut was split in the centre, ami partly b'own

out of the bolt ropes. The ship evidently, so far j as could be observed in the darkness, was aground only at the bows, aud hung by the stern in deep water. The waves were making a clean breach over her amidships. Immediately under the bows of the ship, in a narrow creek formed by the rocks at either side where the force of the tide con- Vice Admiral Sir Charles Napier, K. C. B. : þÿ verged, the strip of sand and shingle, where the shore is very steep, was found literally covered with dead bodies, both male and female, the remains of the unhappy creatures who had endeavoured to save their lives by lotting themselves down by the bow ropes and bowsprit rigging, but who unfortunately wore washed from their hold by the violence of the storm. On either side of the creek the shore was strewn with dead bodies, boxes, packages, parcels, and sea-chests. The remnant of the passengers and crew saved from the wreck wore found encamped in the vicinity of the coast-guard station. Several of the more respectable class had obtained shelter in the coast-guard stationhousc and in the few cottages adjoining ; the great mass of the people

rescued, however, were bevouacked on a grassy hollow under the shelter of a hill, their encampment being fortified with boxes, chests, and parcels of bedding. The coast-guard men had made most praiseworthy exertions to relieve the sufferers. Two of the guard boats had made three trips each to the mainland for the purpose of collecting and bringing off provisions and other necessaries, and it was ascertained that some few of the survivors contrived to reach the mainland by means of fishing boats. As it was quite dark when the gentlemen from the Prince arrived at the creek, and as many of the passengers wore wounded and disabled, it was decided not to attempt their removal until the next day. A message to that effect was accordingly sent on board, and the steamer took up her berth for the night. Can it re True? þÿ þÿ is It a remarkable fact, with reference to the unfortunate vessel, that she underwent no experimental trial previous to her departure from Liverpool for Australia. She was sent out of the docks into the Irish Channel with a valuable cargo, and swarming with human life, and it is stated, that, before she was twenty miles outside of Liverpool, it was discovered that she would not obey her þÿhelm. Romance and Reality. þÿ Among the passengers saved were a man named Carley and his wife, whose adventures invest portions of his history with all the interest marking romance in real life. In the year 1841 he was sentenced at the Rutland Assizes to transportation for 10 years for sheep-slaughtering. At that time he was about to marry a young woman who had þÿ loved not wisely but too þÿwell. She was in attendance in court during his trial, indulging in the anxious hope that the jury would acquit him. The delivery of the sentence was the precursor of a painful scene. She shrieked, threw her arms around the þÿprisoner s neck, and became overpowered with grief. He was, however, sent out of the country, and she was compelled to make stays for the support of herself and a young child, the paternity of which theconvict did not deny. Twelve years passed without the woman receiving any intelligence from Botany Bay. One morning in October last, however, she had been to Morcott on business, and entered a railway carriage for the purpose of returning to Stamford. In

the same compartment were several men, one of whom so intently fixed his eyes upon her that she was induced to change her position in order to escape the apparent rudeness. From the St. Thomas Times, March 4, 1854 1. Johns. Shortly after I forwarded my late communication of 14th ulto., several new eases of Cholera occurred in our Island, chiefly at the Estate þÿ Bevel þÿhoudtsberg, but they were, I am glad to inform you, like the last glimmerings of a flame before it finally expires. Our crest-fallen Planters have, therefore, all reason to hope that the quarantine regulations which have latterly stopped the intercourse between your Island and ours, will be immediately rescinded. Before I proceed from the pathetic to the humorous, permit me to offer my grateful acknowledgements for the space in the St. Thom<t Tidende, which you have gratuitously afforded my communications on Cholera. To my inexpressible amusement I find an article in the columns of the St. Croix Avis wherein I am requested to go back to the year 17fi0 (contemporaneous with my Great-grand-mother) (?) for a reply to iny remarks on St. Croix, (which I shall in future call Bridget) ; and this curious piece of antiquity emanates from (Lord preserve me!) a go-ahead" people! Bridget's þÿ representative farther deplores her þÿ natural barþÿriers, from which, in addition toiler shallowness, she suffers th cNinety-nine Plagues of an empty Purse. Verily, Bridget is like unto the cow that bored herself with her own horn. I confess that the interest I take in your Island prevents me being otherwise than delighted if Bridget, by opening her free port and extending a current of trade, could be made to liquidate per se; such rclief to the body politic would stop the outlet through

which part of your revenue annually ekes, and could, in no wise, injure the colossal trade of your Island ; for, as a Planter waggishly remarks, þÿ as your Harbor is to Port so is Bridget's Basin to Small-beer. St. Johns, 3rd March, 1854. Without taking any interest in the correspondence passing between St. Johns and St Croix, or desiring in any way to participate in it, we may, however, be allowed to remark, with respect to tho writer who alluded to the þÿ vacant þÿlots in our town, that ho was (?) evidently little acquainted with our history, or he would have known that duriug a period of forty years the

town of St. Thomas has been destroyed six times by fire, and twice by hurricane, to wit þÿ 1804, 1806, 1825, 1826, 1832, 1837, by fire; 1819, 1837, by hurricane. The wealth absorbed by those calamities can hardly be estimated. It is enough to know that enumerable families whose descent would have gone down in affluence, were totally kroken up. No wonder then that in spite of all enterprise there should be a few þÿ vacant þÿlots in St. þÿThomas town. þÿ Ed. Tid.

From the Observer, February 12, J854. THE TURt'O-RITSSI 1A AVAR. THE HEJKCTED NEGOTIATIONS. Though tho hopes of peace excited by Count OrlofPs mission wore slight, no one supposed that the Emperor of Russia was about to offer a fresh and di liberate insult to every Court in Europe, by passing over in supercilious silence the exertions which had been made by all the other powers for the restoration of peace, and by intimating that he was himself disposed to treat only on terms radically opposed to every principle which those Powers had recognised and established. Such, nevertheless, is the true character of Count OrlofTs mission, and, now that the propositions of which lie was the bearer have transpired, we can describe them in no language too strong to denote their arrogance and absurdity. The conditions on which Count Oiloff was to express the þÿEmperor readiness s to treat were four in number þÿ that a Turkish plenipotentiary should proceed to the head-quarters of the army or to St. Petersburg to open direct negotiations with Russia, but with liberty to refer to the Ministers of the four Powers; that tho former treaties between Russia and the Porte should be renewed; that Turkey should enter into an engagement not to give an asylum to political refugees ; and that the Porte should recognise, by a declaration, the Russian protectorate of tho Greek Christians, which was tho origin of the quarrel. The Austrian Government did not hesitate to declare to- Count Orloff that those protocols, which had been drawn up by England and France at Count

þÿBuol o s wn request, were the truo basis of the conduct that Minister is resolved to pursue ; that any infraction of those principles would be diehonourable and impolitic ; and that tho Emperor Francis Joseph will adhere to these conditions even at the hazard of war. If any doubt could still exist as to the intentions ot the Emperor Nicholas, even on the part of those who were most disposed to put a favourable construction on his

actions, the tenor of Count OrlolTs propositions must have (lisp 'lied it. Terms of p ace in such shape do not even disguise the vindictive and insatiable passions of war. They were sent not »o much to insure the fall of Turkey as the subjection of Germany. D inands more utterly extravagant it would have been impossible to frame, as far as Turkey is concerned, unless the Czar had required of the Sultan the surrender of his territories and the abdication of his crown ; and, in making these terms the price of peace, the Emperor Nicholas has given t he strongest proof of his determination to persist in war, since he must have been perfectly aware that under no circumstance whatever could the þÿI orte have submitted to them They amount, in fact, to a considerable increase on Piince Monschikoff's demands But the propositions addressed by Nicholas to bis former friends an l allies, the Emp aor of Austria and the King of Prussia, were scarcely less humiliating. Of them ho required an absolute and unconditional armed neutrality in the Eastern quarrel ; hut, a3 if he foresaw and acknowledged that such a neutrality was in fact, a co-operation with his own designs, and would probably expose the German States to the hostility of the Western Powers, he condescended to assure those ancient and power- ! ful monarchies that Russia would protect them ; I and, as a recompense for this service, Count <)rloff was to promise them that in the approaching dissolution of the Ottoman empire their interests I

should not be forgotten. No wonder that on I bearing sudi a communication the Ministers of Austiia auJ Prussia felt an astonishment and irritation they did not disguise ; and that the first impulse of every honest m in cognizant of these transacti ms was to set his name to a declaration that they were peremptorily rejected. It was an attempt on the part of Russia, not only to assert her supremacy over the whole Christian population of the East, and to drag the Turkish Government as a suppliant to St. Petersburg, but also, and, at the sam time, to place the leading Powers of Germany in positive and avowed dependence on the policy of the ( 'zar. If such a scheme could have succeeded, not only would it have rendered war in the East more certain an 1 prolably more protract) d, but it must infallibly have < xtended that war to tli rest of Europe ; it w mid instantly have divided the German and the Western Powers into two camps, and, while they were contending i'or a cause not their own, Russia would have found herself at liberty to act as she pleased on the Danube and the Euxine. If that was the Russian plan, we must be permitted to lay that it was a diabolical attempt to aggravate it hundredfold the evils wo a'rcady owe to her i rapacity and ambition. But the snare was too evident and flic bait too clumsy to deceive any one. The Czar appears to have formed an equally low estimate of the morality and the intelligence of his dupes. ORIGIN OF THE NAVAL POWER OF RUSSIA. It was not the Czar Peter who founded the Muscovite navy þÿ it was his father Alexis. That good prince was then the ally of Persia, and, to facilitate trade with that country, which his successors have since treated so well, lie endeavoured to establish maritime communications on the Caspian Sea, which has since become a Russian lake, in all the force of the term. Carpenters were engaged by his orders in Holland. In addition to numerous trading vessels, they built for him at Dcdnoff, on the Oka, a vessel of war called the Eagle. But the Eagle was burnt in the revolt of tho Cossack chief, Stcnko-Unzin, and, according to Voltaire, in his History of C/uirlcs XII. t the word þÿ fleet was unknown in tho

3 0 Ji b 2 A T at 3 Russian language up to the time of Peter the Great, the founder of the Selavonian power, who creati d both the word and the thing He had first of all, at the mouth of the Veronise, two vessels constructed iti 1689 by Dutchmen and Venetians, and shortly after lie thought of dominating in the Black Sea. The Turks have always committed the fault þÿ and the affair of Sinope is one proof of it of not sufficiently occu- þÿ pying themselves with the Black Sea. In those times they principally occupied themselves with the Mediterranean and the Archipelago, whilst they ought to have paid equal at tenth in to the Mediterranean and the Euxine An empire like the Ottoman empire had the means of keeping in the latter sea a fleet capable of checking the development of another navy. It would have escaped many misfortunes had it done so. But it seems that it never dreaded misfortunes from the East, and that it always expected them from the opposite side. Peter the Great perfectly saw the situation. In 1696, his little navy had already become a large fleet, which served to take Azoff, and with Azoff to give him a very great influence in the Black Sea. Some years later, this fleet ; consisted of fifty vessels, bearing from 30 to 60 cannons, and Russian officers served on board of them with a multitude of foreign adventurers, after having studied for a short time in Holland, at Venice, and Leghorn. Every one knows how Peter Michaeloff himself at Saai dutu directed the construction of a vessel of 60 guns, which he sent

ready fitted out to Archangel þÿ he wishing to have his northern fleet, as well as his western and eastern fleets At that time tho princes vied with each other in encouraging Russia. King William gave to Peter Michaeloff another vessel called the Royal Transport, ami all at once the carpenter, again become Czar, took with him 3 captains, 23 sailing-masters, 40 surgeons, 230 gunners, and a still larger number of sailors. Europe has always acted in this way þÿ she has never ceased to give the barbarian powers the means of defeating her. She ought, however, to have divined the projects of tho Czar Peter from the activity of his foundations. In some years lie built 8t. Petersburg, and Cronslot, founded Taganrog, and, constantly going and coining, studied all the shores of the Baltic. There was not a difficult passage which lie did not sound himself. II is most confidential friends did the same for the Black Sea. The Turks, however, had a good chance of injuring him after his disaster on the Pruth, but they did not go far enough. By the treaty of Falksen, they con- 6 nti d themselves with making him give up Azuff, with the ammunition and artillery which that place contained before the capture, and with destroying the foundations of Taganrog. As to the fleet, they committed the mistake of leaving it in all its force. It was quiet for some time. However this may be, thus cheeked in his development to the East, Peter the Great endeavoured to gain towards the north what the Turks took

from him on their part. The struggle with the tjo enterprising Charles XII., afforded him the means. The Swedes were not then the excellent sailors they are now. Charles XII., and his predecessors, always cutcrptising on the continent, had turned their whole attention to the land forces, and by a fault similar to that of the Turks, had almost completely neglected to protect themselves against a Russian navy. The latter, however, had considerably increased, so much so that Peter the Great attempted with it the conquest of the isle of Aland. þÿ He þÿleft, says the historian of the King of Sweden, þÿ on his expedition at the commencement of July, 1714, while, his rival Charles XII., remained in his bed at Dcmotica. He embarked at the port of Cronslot, which he had built some years before at fou miles from St. Petersburg. The new port, tbo fleet which it contained, the officers and sailors who manned that fleet þÿ all were his work ; and

on whatever side he east his eyes, he saw nothing which he had not, as it were, created. The Russian fleet arrived on the 15th July near Aland; it consisted of 30 vessels of the line, of 80 galleys, and 100 small galleys. It conveyed 20,000 soldiers. Admiral Apraxin commanded it, and the Russian E uperor served as Rear-Admiral. The Swedish fleet met it on the 16th; it was commanded by Vice-Admiral Eiinschild, and was less strong by two-thirds. Nevertheless it fought for three hours. The Czar attacked the vessel of Eiinschild and took it after an obstinate combat. On the day of the victory lie disembarked 16,000 soldiers in Aland, and having taken several Swedish soldiers who had not been able to embark in the fleet of Eiinschild, lie carried them prisoners to bis vessels. He re-entered the port of Cronslot with the large vessel of tho þÿenemy s admiral, three others of less force, a frigate, and six galleys, which he had taken. From Cronslot lie conveyed bis prizes to St. þÿPetersburg. This was the first naval triumph of the Russians, but it was an easy one. This victory of Aland made a great noise. It led to an English fleet being sent to the Baltic, and at one moment it was feared in Russia that the taking of the Swedish island would be dearly revenged. Rut the English did n it understand the danger which arose to the world from this first success. They despised tho Russian navy, and only saw, in their relations witli the North, the passing interests of their commerce. The market of Russia was

greater and richer than that of Sweden, whi' h was then ruined. It turned its back to that State, which, reduced to itself, was very happy to conclude the treaty of Nystadt, which gave to Russia the domination of the Baltic. þÿ Ibid.

Tit rot Tat. þÿ It is stated in a letter from St. Petersburg, that the Czar, on learning that the protocol of the 13th Jan. had the signature of the Austrian Emperor, exclaimed þÿ John Sobieski and Nicholas the First have been tho most ill-advised kings of Poland : the one delivered Vienna from the Turks, and tho other saved it from the þÿHungarians. Mistake of the Czar. þÿ It is now felt (according to a St. Petersburg letter) to be a great j mistake on the part of Russia, that a sufficient force was not sent in the spring of last year to settle affairs with Turkey, as the prolonged contest is full of financial difficulties for Russia, besides leading to complications with the West. English Officers. þÿ It was currently reported among the military on the Danube, that the Russians declare the Turkish artillery to be directed by English officers ; that it is out of the question that Turks could fire in the manner they have done at Oltenitza and Csitatc unassisted. This is paying an unintentional compliment to their practice, for, excepting four or five Prussian instructors, none of whom have served in batteries in action since tho commencement of the war, the Turkish artillery is officered and manned entirely by Turks. Arad Feeling. þÿ The animosity of the Moslem against the Christians appears to have completely disappeared. The Arabs of the desert held a general meeting under the direction of tho Sheiks, at which they made a solemn vow to forget their private quarre's during the war, and if
one tribe committed any depredations, the other would unite and punish them.

We Frederik the Seventh, by the grace of God Kim of Denmark, the Vandals and the Gotha, Duke i>f Sleswig, Hoislcen, Stonnarn, D.lmarsh, Lunenburg amt Oldenburg, Make known ; On the report ot Our Minister of Finance who has laid before Us tiie deliberation of the Colonial Council on a Dralt of Ordinance for the prevention of Vagrancy in Our YVestindia Possessions, We most graciously decree : þÿ L Persons who are not known to possess property, nor to have any fixed livelihood, nor any situation in life, which guarantees, that they find their sustenance without detriment to the public, shall be called before tho Police-Magistrate to give an account of the manner ia which they support themselves. If , the explanation giver, such individual 52- by proves unsatisfactory, either by itself or on furiher invcsimation, the Police Magistrate shall order him -such or. der to be duly put on þÿrecord to seek some lawful means of support, allowing him a certain time within which lie is to appear and prove that the order has been complied with, and also warn him, that in default thereof he will be punished as a Vagrant. The Police-Magistrate is authorised to dictate to the Individual the observance of such rules, by w hich the Police shall be enabled to control, that the order given is complied with and that the intent and purpose thereof bo actually attained ; therefore if the individual h» considered lit for any regular employment as houseservant, field-laborer, sea -man, apprentice, or the like,

the Police-Magistrate ran order bun to accept such employment, if he can obtain the same, or, in want thereof, if it can be obtained for him by the Police. The circumstance of the individual being married and actually residing with his family shall lie duly considered, as far as consistent w ith the purpose of this enactment. If the Individual in question do wilfully neglect tha injunctions given accordingly, he shall be punished a a Vagrant. 5 3gressions of the Laws, and also in Police-Cases rela- In cases of public investigation respecting transtive to offences against property, fights or brawls, or concerning the relation between employers and laborers, masters and servants, the Police-Magistrates shall avail themselves of the opportunity for demanding elucidations respiting the domicile ami livelihood of tlicso persons, who may be implicated and of whom no suf. ticicnt knowledge is at hand, in order to ascertain how far therule8 laid down in the 1st and 2nd ) of this ordinance are applicable to them. If during any judicial investigation, that is not carried on by the Police-Magistrate, there appear circumstances leading to suppose, that an individual has no lawful means of support, the judge shall give written communication thereof to tiie Police-Magistrate. 5 4- Persons without occupation, who have been released after having undergone their punishment of imprisonment or public-work, are then in accordance with the 2nd to be enjoined to seek lawful occupation.

Accordingly, those persons entitled to receive such bonds, cither as owners of emancipated unfree or in

Christiansted, Friday the 3 lit March 1854 It 18 now a long time since we have seen Chimney-sweepers employed, and we think that some, if not all, of the chimneys here in town require sweeping. This duty, although apparently very simple, ought not to be neglected. It is not improbable that the soot in one or other of these chimneys may ignite, and before it is discovered, cause an incalculable loss of property, and even the loss of lives. We hope that owners of houses will turn their attention to this, and have their chimneys cleaned.

I Parents belonging to the country-population shall not commit their young children, or such as are yet Bound to frequent school, to the care of persons in tho towns, unless such persons are considered by the Police-Magistrate to possess such means, that the main- to tenance and education of such children in time cotne can be secured, þÿ after which the necessary stipulations in this respect, and especially as regards the schooling of the child, shall be entered into by the parties concerned before the Police-Magistrate. authority for approbation.

6. bound Every owner of a house or of landed such to render to the Police-Magistrate property is information concerning persons residing on their property, as may be demanded ; and to report to the Police all removals, within 48 hours.

The punishment for Vagrancy for such persons who have not formerly been found guilty thereof, shall be imprisonment on bread and water from 48 to 4 times 48 hours with legal intervals. 8. When any person, having once been convicted for | vagrancy, is again found guilty thereof, the punishment shall according to circumstances be imprisonment on bread and water from 5 to 10 times 48 hours, and i in case of further repetition from 10 to 15 times 48 j hours. It shall be optional with the judge, whenever such punishment appears to be more suitable, to apply imprisonment with hard labour instead of imprisonment on bread and water, so that in lieu of 48 hours of such imprisonment there shall be awarded imprisonment with hard labor for 12 days. If the Individual be again convicted of the same offence, the punishment shall be imprisonment with hard labor from 6 to 12 months, and for each repetition thereof, the term of such imprisonment shall be further extended, lrowever in no case beyond 2 years. $ 9. Children and other individuals under 18 years of age, who wilfully leave the situation or occupation, to which they have been bonnd by their parents or other persons concerned, shall be kept to the observance of their duties by proper chastisements, and if the individual be of an age between 15 and 18 years, then punishment according to the 1st of the Ordinance of 23rd May 1840 concerning imprisonment on bread and water, can be awarded, if required by circumstances. 10. Persons, who cannot legally be considered as Va-

grants, but who are discovered to have taken abode during tho night in yards, galleries, sheds, carriagehouses or such other places, where they have no right to stay, shall be subject to a fine or to imprisonment for some days, provided their conduct does otherwise not make them liable to higher punishment. 11. Owners or occupiers of houses, neglecting to make the report ordered in $ 6 respecting the removal of persons, shall be subject to a fine from 50 Cents to 5 dollars for each case. Persons wilfully harbouring Vagrants, and any person wilfully returning incorrect reports or entering into fictitious agreements in order to conceal transregulations concerning gressions or elusions of the this ordinance or of any other matters of labor or service, Shall be fined from 1 to 10O dollars. In cases of repetition the fine may be doubled. 12. All cases concerning transgressions of this ordinance shall be dealt with and bo decided by the Police Courts. 13. All former enactments regarding Vagrancy in the Danish Weslindia possessions not consistent with this ordinance, are repealed. ( 14. The Governor of onr Westindia possessions is authorised to fix the day on which this ordinanco shall como into operation. To which all concerned have to conform. Prom the Observer, March 12, 1854. The Baltic fleet weighed anchor from Spithead yes terday at half-past two o'clock, and never a fleet went to sea under happier auspices. The fleet is most powerful, and well equipped. The Commander-in-Chief is approved by the people, no less than by the Government, who remember his past deeds. The Queen and her people assembled to bid them God speed þÿ and all of us join in the general blessing. They have gone to sea in good spirits, and well found in every way, and seem to be favoured by Providence in the good causo by the most favourable þÿgales the wind blowing South West. Fresh and Gentle Gales, precisely in tho right quarter. They are gone in a just cause, and with the blessings of an entire people, who arc unanimous in wishing the brave Tars a good voyage, victory, and a speedy return to " happy homes and a triumphant altars free."

PRUSSIA The King of Prussia has put his army on a war footing. He has divided that army into three grand divisions, the first of which is stationed in the Baltic provinces, the second in Silesia , and the third on tho Rhine. The first two of these divisions are numerically very strong, and are composed of Prussia's finest troops. The smallest division is the one on the Rhine This disposition of the Prussian army is considered as a clear indication'tliat, in the event of actual hostilities, Prussia does not mean to be neutral. She places the main body of her forces, not towards the frontiers of France, but towards those of Russia. That Russia sees the attitude assumed by Prussia in an unfavourable light, is evident from the disposition she has made of her army in Poland. That corps d'armf.e, which was in (the first instance under orders to join the army of the Danube, has had those orders countermanded, and it now remains stationary in Poland. This change in the plans of the Czar is not in consequence of any apprehension of a rising in Poland þÿ for that country is quiet, and the Czar is adopting other measures in the hope of keeping it quiet; neither can it be for the purpose of repelling any danger of invasion by the English or French, by means of the Baltic fleet, for the Polish provinces are too far from the scene of opera tions. The only reason, therefore, for leaving so important a body of troops in Poland, while their servicei are required elsewhere, is to watch Prussia, with whose
intentions the Czur is by no means satisfied. þÿ Ibid, March 6

OPENING OF THE FRENCH CHAMBERS. f BY SUBMARINE AND EUROPEAN TELEGRAPH.) (FROM OI'R own correspondent ) PARIS, Friday The Emperor has opened the Chambers in person. After having spoken at length on the insufficiencv of the last harvest, and the means taken to provide for the deficiency, the Emperor said þÿ þÿ Last year, in my opening discourse, I promised to use every effort in my power to maintain peace and to re-assurc Europe. I have kept my word. In order to avoid a struggle, I have deferred it as long as was permitted by honour. Europe will know now, beyond doubt, that if France has drawn the sword, it is only because >he has been constrained to do so. She will know that. France has no idea of aggrandisement. She wishes only to resist dangerous pretensions. Thus I love to proclaim aloud that the time for conquests is passed, never to return, for it is not by reducing boundaries that a nation can henceforth be honoured and powerful : it is self at the head of generous ideas, by in placing the causing herwill perceive the results of a prevail without tism and without arriere pensee. It is thus ego- empire of law and justice to policy ; in this you that | England, our ancient rival, forms with us an alliance from day to day more strict and more intimate, because the ideas which we defend arc the same as those of the English people. Germany, which the remembrance of former wars still I renders suspicious, and which for that reason perhaps has given for the last forty years too many

8 tr, V'Ji OU ATI 8proofs of deference to the policy of the cabinet of St. Petersburgh, has already recovered her independence from its allurements, and freely regards in what quarter her interests are to be found. Austria, above all, which cannot see with indifference the events which are preparing, enters into our alliance, and thus will confirm the character of morality and justice which marks the war which we undertake. This is, indeed, the reason why she engages in it. Europe, engaged in intestine struggles for forty years, re-assured, also, by the moderation of the Emperor Alexander in 1815, as by that of his successor until this day, seemed not to dread the danger which might menace her from the collossal power which, by her successive encroachments, embraces the north and the south þÿ which possesses almost exclusively the two interior seas from which she can dart fortli upon our civilisation. It sufficed, by the advance of an ill-founded pretension at Constantinople, to awaken sleeping Europe. þÿ We have seen, in effect, in the East, amidst profound peace, a Sovereign exact from his most feeble neighbour new advantages, and because

vinces. þÿ This fact ought to make those who revolt against iniquity take up arms ; but wo have other reasons for supporting Turkey. France has as much and perhaps more interest than England that the influence of Russia should not extend \ surprise, and cut them to indefinitely in Constantinople, for to reign over Constantinople is to reign over the Mediterranean, and not one of you, gentlemen, l think, will say that England alone has great interests in that sea which washes 300 leagues of our coasts. Besides this, that policy does not date from yesterday. For ages every national government in France has supported it, and I will not desert it. Let it no longer he said that we have leagued together to go to Constantinople with England only to defend the cause of the Sultan, and with it the rights of the Christians. We go there to defend the liberty of the seas and our just influence in the M iditerranean ; we go with Germany to aid her to preserve the rank from which it seemed to be desired to make her descend, to guard her frontiers against the preponderance of too powerful a neighbour ; we go, in line, with all those who desire the triumph of good, of law, of justice, and of civilisation. þÿ In these solemn circumstances, gentlemen, as in all those in which I shall be obliged to appeal to the country, I am sure of your support ; for I have always found in you the generous sentiments which animate the nation. Thus strong in this support, in the nobleness of the cause, and
in the sincerity of our alliances, and confiding, above all, in the protection of God, L hope soon to obtain a peace which it will not he in the power of any one to disturb with þÿimpunity.

BATTLE IN THE DARK. On the 17th of February a curious conflict took place by mistake at night between two columns of the Russian army. The Turkish positions are extended in an easterly direction as the village of Cuiperceni, which is about a mile distant from Kalafat. For several days a Turkish corps, 4,000 strong, under the command of Colonel Mirolai, had been posted in front of this village, and in the direction of the Russian outposts j On this corps the Russians resolved to make an onslaught during the night of the 16th, and to drive it hack within the Turkish lines ; or, at any rate, they meant thus to commence their operations against Kalafat itself. For this purpose they were not obtained invading two of her pro- : two Russian columns ivere brought up, each from j 4,000 to 5,000 men strong þÿ one by the road which leads to Kalafat, from about the village of Seribczi, and the other from the left side of it, from about Poisna (Prince þÿMilosch sproperty), to advance unexpectedly upon the Turks, enclose, pieces The Russian columns commenced their march at three þÿo clock in the morning, and by about four a. m , the former of them reached a position from whence they were only half an þÿhour smarch from the Turkish pickets. The second column seems either to have missed the direction by mistaking the road, or to have come up long after its time Be this as it may, the latter column, in the obscurity of a foggy night, concluded the former one to be the body of hostile Turks, and instantly

opened upon them w i t li a terrific cannonade, which the others, who laboured under the same mistake, returned with yet more deadly effect. Pressing towards each other, it came ere long to a close fire of small arms. This ill-omened combat lasted for upwards of an hour and a half, until, when at length day dawned, the combatants saw with horror the error they had committed. The loss in killed and wounded in the course of this þÿnight encounter s is reckoned (by the Russians themselves) at several hundreds. The Turks were naturally alarmed at þÿeY erv point , and at \\ iddin, which is hut a league ami a half distant, Omer Pacha, on hearing the cannonado, took all the requisite measures for defence. The Turkish corps stationed at Cuiperceni stood to arms, in readiness for action at any moment, hut did not advance as it was at a loss to imagine or comprehend what the Russians were about, murdering one another in that style. It was only between six and seven þÿo clock a. m., that tho Russian columns withdrew to their respective positions after their fight.

On the 17th (the French official declaration of war having arrived, without which Admiral Hamelin was naturally unwilling to proceed to extremities) both fleets sailed for Odessa, before which place they anchored on the afternoon of the 20th. An explanation was demanded of General Osten Sacken, the military governor here, as to his reasons for outraging a flag of truce, always held sacred by all nations pretending to civilisation. DENMARK The elite, of the aristocracy of Copenhagen, several high placemen and military officers, the cream of le beau monde, were invited, a few days since, by Sir Charles to breakfast, on hoard his own ship. It took some time to convince themselves that the former, present, or future position of the persons in question allowed them to accept an invitation, which might take the stamp of an anti-

Russian demonstration ; it was, how ever finally agreed on, and the steamer Skjbld, lay, early the next morning, ready to take the beauty, elegance, and riches of the capital on board to Sir Charles. They emhar ed in the best humour, in the hope of passing a delightful day, when suddenly, the startling report was heard, that the fleet had disappeared, and that even with the best telescopes, it was no longer possible to discover the proud squadron that had lain so long in Kidge Bay. Nothing was heard hut expressions of despair and ill-will towards the impolite English Admiral. The only resource now was to return home. It was quite impossible to make a voyage of discovery after the fleet, and perhaps not overtake it and the breakfast before they came to Gothland or even to Cronstadt. They consequently separated with considerably longer faces than when they met. Some of the company, however, took advantage of the clear morning, and went to enjoy the air at Eungelinie, and there, to their no little joy, they found that the þÿ Duke of þÿWellington was still laying in the hay, waiting for his guests Sir Charles had, early in the morning, ordered the fleet to weigh anchor, and go a little to the south, in order to give his guests an opportunity of witnessin r the beautiful sight of a whole fleet ready for battle sailing towards the þÿshore. From the Observer, May 14, 1854 THE DANUBE The silence which has for some time past been observed in the march of events on the Danube is now at length broken. Intelligence h.sbeen received in official quarters, and gradually leaked out, that the Russians are getting too strong for Omar Pacha, that they appear in force along the coast from Matchin to Kustendje, that they have occupied the positiou of þÿTrajan s Wall, where they are throwing up entrenchments ; that they are preparing to lay siege to Silistria ; and that in a very short time, perhaps, they will threaten \ arna. Omar Pasha is hampered by bands of predatory irregulars, and sadly in want of heavy artillery and money to pay his troops. For either of them his requests have been urgent, but void of success. There is a regiment of artillery and 120 heavy cannon lying idle in the artillery barracks at Pera, but for some reason or other the þÿSultan best s general is left to fight the Russians as best he may, and the safety of the empire is sacrificed to the petty intrigues and personal resentments of the Porte. Part, of the English and French troops at Gal lipoli have been directed upon Adrianople. It is impossible to give an idea of the irregularity and uncertainty of the dislocation of troops þÿ even the staff officers and commissioners know little or nothing of what is going on, and every day some false rumour, emanating from officers who from their position arc supposed to have correct information, misleads the public as to the strength and the names of the regiments that are

going to join. When Messrs. Hory and Grant, archivists of the French nnd English consulates at Bucharest, took their departure, a gentleman employed in the English consulate was arrested by order of General Budberg, and sent, to Bender. M. Rotta is a Roumeliotc by birth, and has been four years in the service of the English consulate. When he was appointed archivist, Prince Stirbey refused to recognise him in that character, and he remained in consequence a simple attache. The arrest of M. Rotta is an additional proof that the Czar never hesitates to violate the law of nations The Turks resorted to a ruse dt guerre lately at Silistri, in enticing over a body of the enemy across the river. They set fire to a huge pile of reeds, straw, and dry weeds, which looked as if the town was in flames. Loud hurrahs resounded in the Russian camp ; they thought the moment favourable for crossing, and hoped in the confusion to carry either the whole or a part of the fortress by a coup dt main. But the Turks had already planted an ambuscade of sufficient strength in the vineyard near the town, along which the Russians would have to pass. A contest ensued, and the Russians had to retreat, being both out,generalled and overmatched.

A supplement extraordinary to the Journal de St. Petersburg of April 1 1 ( 3rd) contains the following manifesto : þÿ Sr. Petersburg, April 11 (23rd.) þÿ lly the grace of God we, Nicholas the First, Emperor and Autocrat ot all the Russias, King of Poland, &c., &.C., to all our subjects make known Since the þÿ ; commencement of our difference with the Turkish Government we have solemnlv announced to our faithful subjects "that a sentiment of justice had alone induced us to re-establish the violated rights of the orthodox Christians, subjects of the Ottoman Porte. We have not sought, we do not seek, to make conquests, nor to exercise in Turkey any supremacy whatever that might be likely to exceed that influence which belongs to Russia by virtue of existing treaties. At that period we already encountered distrust', then soon a covert hostility on the part of the Governments of France and England, who endeavoured to lead the Porte astray by misrepresenting our intentions. Lastly at this moment, England and France throw off the mask, remere secondary question, gard our difference with and Turkey as a no longer dissemble that their joint object is to weaken Russia, to tear from her a part of her possessions, and to bring down our country from the powerful position to which the hand of the Supreme Reing had exalted it. Is it for orthodox Russia to fear such threats ? Ready to confound the audacity ot the the enemy, shall she swerve from the

sacred purpose that has been assigned to her by Divine Providence? No! Russia has not forgotten God ! It is not for arms. worldly interests that for She combats she has taken lip the Christian faith, for the defence of her co-religionists oppressed by implacable enemies. Let all Christendom know, then, that the thought of the Sovereign of Russia is also the thought that animates and sian people þÿ inspires all the great family of the faith- this orthodox people, Rusful to God and to His only Son, Jesus Christ our Redeemer. It is for the faith and for Christendom that we combat ! God with us þÿ who against ns? Given at St. Petersburg, on the 11 lb grace 1854, day of the month of 29th and the April, in the year of of our reign. NICHOLAS.

The members of the Colonial Council for the Danish West India Possessions assembled at Government House for the opening of its second session, ou Friday the 2nd of -Tune 1854 at 11 þÿo clock. The Governor opened the meeting with an introductory speech, in which he called the attention of the Council to the gracious and confiding reception with which the propositions of the Council had mot at the hands of His Majesty the King, in which respect he referred to the two following communications from the Government. He dwelt upon the severe trials, which these colonies have had to undergo since the closure of the first session, from epidemics as well as from unfavorable crops, while the prospects for the future were more cheering. He observed that all elucidations which the committees, that may be

© IK © 2 A T 1 8« appointed on the divers matters to be discussed by the Council, would be given on application to himself ; þÿ he notified, that the 5th Member for St. Thomas District was, by business which admitted of no delay, prevented from meeting for some days, and concluded, in behalf of His Majesty the King, by declaring the second session of the Colonial Council opened. The communications produced by the Government run as follows : COMMUNICATION I Vo in I lie Government to the Colonial Council. The Minister of Finance has by a Letter, dated the 2Gth of September 1853, transmitted to the Government a Royal Rescript of the following contents :

We FKEDER1K the Seventh, by the Grace of God, King of Denmark, the Vandals and the Goths, Duke of Sleswick, Holstein, Stormarn, Ditmarsh, Lauenburg and Oldenburg, Our Greeting ! The dutiful representations of

sions, assembled in the Year 1852, having been laid before Us by Our Minister of Finance, We graciously charge You to make known | to the Colonial Council at their next Session, that We have with satisfaction observed, that Our expectations are justified by the intelligent and | honest exertions of the Council for the welfare of the Colonies, and also to commuuicate to the Colonial Council the result of the decisions adopted ou each of the matters dutifully represented to Us by them, as follows: The Laws and Ordinances mentioned hereafter, Drafts of which have been laid before the Colonial Council, have beeu promulgated, viz : On the 23rd of July this year þÿ A Law regarding the Compensation to be given to the former Owners of Unfree in the Danish W est India Possessions. On the 31st July this þÿyear A Law granting a supplement to the Budget for 1853-54 concerning the Revenues and Expenses of the Colonies. On the 18th August this þÿyear An Ordinance to prevent Vagrancy in the Danish West India Possessions. On the same date þÿ An Ordinance, containing Provisions for regulating the relations between Masters aud Servants in the Danish West India Possessions. On the Gth of the present month þÿ An Ordinance regulating trades and professions in the Danish West India Possessions. On the 6th of the present month þÿ An Ordinance containing regulations for the Country Schools in the Dauish West India Possessions. In accordance with the proposal of the Colonial Council, We have considered it expedient, that

the Ordinance, regarding the relations between the Proprietors of landed Estates and laborers in the Danish West India Possessions, of which a draft has been laid before the Council, should not be put in force. At the same time We have directed Our Minister of Finance to cause inquiries, regarding the Regulations that should he established, relative to the medical attendance on Estates, aud the measures that should be adopted, to secure the support of those persons, who from age or infirmity are unable to work on the Estates ; also to communicate to the Government the needful, regarding divers propositions contained in the above-mentioned Draft, for the better determination of the rules, now regulating this matter. Wo will also, if any special regulations concerning laborers from foreign countries be proposed by the Colonial Cbuncil, take into consideration, how far it may be necessary or expedient to legislate on that matter. In regard to the Draft of Ordinance respecting the extension to the Danish West India Posses-

We copy from the St. Thomas i ministry, Times of the 31st May the following Danish news : þÿ A special correspondent of the þÿ Morning þÿHerald, ! in a letter from Copenhagen, dated May 8, says þÿ The Copenhagen paper the Fadreland of May i 8, contain the following paragraph : þÿ þÿ The Morning Chronicle, under date Copenhagen April 21, has stated. þÿ The Finish sailors liberated from the prizes have been treated with unnecessary barbarity. These poor men have been completely plundered. They have been stripped of everything in the shape of money, and flung upon a foreign shore entirely destitute. A merchant of the place, who has large commercial transactions with Finland has kindlv assisted them. He has advanced their passage-money and other necessary sums on his own risk þÿI þÿ Since this paragraph of the Morning Chronicle has found its way into the Danish papers, and probably into those of other nations on the Continent, and is disseminated through the world bv this I/indon journal, it is due to truth, and to the officers of the English navy, that a contradiction should be given, and we arc in a position to supply a refutation of the calumny from a well-informed source. þÿ It is not only false that the Finlanders were flung upon a foreign shore entirely destitute ; but it is true that many of them landed with considerable sums of money, of which no person attempted to deprive them. One of them had £50 and another no less than £150 in his possession. þÿ Captain Carnegie was so anxious that every sailor

should retain everything that was his private property, that he himself superintended the distribution, and was particularly careful that not one of them should lose anything. þÿ We cannot understand how the Morning Chronicle could say that tho Finlanders wero supplied with money for their return by a Copenhagen merchant. Tho Chronicle ought to have known that there is not only a Russian Consul at Copenhagen, but that there i also a Russian Embassy, and (hat in such circum-

stances tho subjects of the Czar need not apply to foreigners for assistance. This part of the story is as false as the rest, and is a pendant to the tale of the Libert as, Captain Raas or Rus, for, from what we know we can state that the English have not taken any vessel of that name, and that consequently it could not have been retaken by the Russians either by stratagem or by þÿforce. ff you refer to the Morning Chronicle you will see the attack upon the English fleet was more extended than the quotation. Rut the above is a literal translation from a Danish newspaper, in which a Dane, who with a manly remembrance of þÿEngland visits s to Copenhagen in 1807, received Admiral þÿNapier s fleet without a cheer, now, with a loyalty as honourable, crushes a reptile, whose slime might have tarnished the reputation of one of þÿNapier brave s companions : þÿ þÿ We could not cheer the English fleet (says a Danish naval captain) ; we could not give a cheer to Napier or hi- fleet, for all our knowledge of England and her naval power is mixed with sad remembrances. But we know how to treat brave rnen. Napier has done nothing yet for us which can claim from us one solitary hurrah. Let him bring the Russian fleet to Copenhagen, and we will find cheers that shall drown every recollection of the terrible storm of 1807. In the meantime be sure that no Dane would slander him or his comrades. There are Englishmen who owe everything they possess to their þÿcountry institutions, s which have enabled them to attain in" other lands a

position they never could have reached in their own ; and who, nevertheless, feed in their hearts a knawing jealous hatred of all who have found and followed the road to honour more successfully than themselves. It is one of þÿNapier own s countrymen who is the inventor of the falsehood, and it is an English newspaper that is the propagator of the þÿslander. In one of the Copenhagen papers of the 9th it is said : þÿ þÿ To the reclamations already made, both by members of the Danish Parliament and by tho princes who believe themselves to have a right to the throne, the Prince Wasa has now added his formal protest against the Law of Succession promulgated by the Danish ministry 31st July, 1853. þÿ The Prince Gustavus of Wasa is the grandson of the Princess Sophia Magdalena of Denmark, wife of Gustavus III., King of Sweden; and is' as is also the present King, Frederik VII., a lineal descendant in the third degree from the Danish King, Frederik V. He is a Field Marshal in the Austrian service, and well advanced in years; but his daughter, the Princess Caroline of Wasa, was married last year to Prince Frederik Albert of Saxony. \\ e recollect that diplomacy has taken good care that the reconciliation as , tliey wish to call it, of Russia, is worth nothing, except so far as the male descendants of the Princess Louise are concerned, and that the younger branches of the house of Oldenburg have equally reserved their rights upon Holstein, if these descendants should become

the Prince of Wasa has put forward his protest, and can percoive that these several reservations will complete themselves by degrees, and altogether, will at length force upon the sight and the understanding of every one the fault of the Danish whosaeriticed without any equivalent, the right of succession to Denmark and Schleswig of the female descendant of tho Princess þÿLouise.

VW i> Revolution in New Grenada. We have been kindly favored with newspapers from Aspinwnll. Panama, and Carthagena, from the latter of which we learn that a revolution had broken out at Bogota, on the. 16th April, headed by General Jose Mn. Melo, who had seized the President, Vice- President and other officials, at the Capital, and declared himself Dictator of the Reþÿpublic. The movement seems to have taken the Republic by surprise, as most of the principal places were unconnected with it. Rarranquilla, Mompox, Santa Martha, and Savanilla, had declared in favor of the deposed administration, and Generals Mosquera and Herrera were actively engaged in raising forces in support of the same cause. General Herrera, and many other members of Congress, saved themselves from the capital with considerable difficulty, but were expected shortly to be able to march on Bogota with a sufficient force to put down the Revolution. þÿ Jamaica Despatch.

The second meeting of the Council was held Saturday, 2nd of June at 11 þÿo clock. The Governor presented the following drafts of laws : 1 ) Draft of a Muuicipai ordinance for the Danish Westindia Possessions He referred to the unsatisfactory provisions laid down in the Rescript of Sth April 17(18, which rendered a new organisation of the Burgher Councils, in accordance with the demands of the present times, and in analogy of the legislation of the mother country, absolutely necessary 2) Draft of au ordinance directing that marriage shall not entitle laborers to dissolve their contracts in the Danish Westindia Possessions. 3) Draft regarding Medical attendance on estates. 4) Draft concerning taxes in the island of St. Thomas. o) Draft of an ordinance concerning an Extra Tax to cover the expenses of the Land Treasury of St. Thomas, caused by the Cholera Epedemic, which amount to $23,500. The Council then entered upon the preliminary discussions of the Draft of a law on trade and navigation in St. Thomas The first Member for Frederiksteds District

HeilbutliJ having made some remarks regarding the division of the ship dues into 4 separate ones, of which at least 3 probably may be consolidated into one, as also on the importation into St. Croix of produce from St. Thomas and St. Johns, his j proposition of having the matter referred to a Committee of 5 was accepted ; elected were : Messrs. Glisten with 18, þÿ Itiisc with 17, þÿ Stenersen with lb, þÿ Heilbuth with 16, þÿ .Birch with 9 votes The discussion on the Budget was, in consequence of a proposal by the 2nd member for Frederiksted Newton, referred to a Committee of 6, to which were elected Messrs. Arnesen with 16, þÿ Newton with 14, | þÿ Castonier with 13, u Glisten with 12 þÿ Friderichsen with 10 votes. At the preliminary discussion on the draft regarding the new organisation of the Upper Court, the Chairman made over his functions to the Vice Chairman. The first Member for Christiansted Arnesen, oconded by the 1st for Froderiksted Ilcilbuth |, proposed : that the further deliberation on this draft should be entrusted to a Committee of 3. The 3rd Member for Frederikstcd PetersenJ observed, on the reservation of his right of a further and more detailed exposition of his views on the subject, that he considered an institution as the Upper Court one of too great importance to be regulated, as done in this case, from a mere financial point of view, and that those motives on which the ordinance of 25th of May 1804 were based, ought yet to be predominant and decisive.

He proposed that a Committee of 5 be appointed, which proposal was seconded by the 1st Member for Christiansted Arnesen j , accepted by the Council, and the following members elected: Messrs. Arnesen with 17, þÿ Ilcilbuth with 17, þÿ Petersen with 15, þÿ llanschell with 13, þÿ Birch with 7 votes. The meeting adjourned at 11 þÿo clock

The third meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday the 6th of June 1854 at 11 þÿo clock. The Governor produced the following drafts of laws : 1 ) Draft of a law regarding the transmission : that the requisite preparatory labours for the extension to the Colonies of the post-ordinances for Denmark had been framed by an official of the Post Department in Copenhagen, in conjunction with the Secretary of the Colonial Government Mr. Birch, and that this gentleman, on account of his more detailed knowledge of the case, would represent him, the Governor, during the discussions of this matter, however with the reservation of his right of voting as member of the Council. 2) Draft of an Grdinance concerning several Taxes in the island of St. Croix to the band Treasury. By the means of these imposts, partly the present debts contracted, and partly the annual deficiency of said þÿTreasury s revenues would be covered. And in conjunction herewith was produced : 3) Draft of law relative to the Tax on Buildings in the Danish Westindia Possessions. The Governor notified, that the protocols containing the new measurement of the buildings of the towns, had been laid on the table in the þÿCouncil s reading room. 4) Draft of law prohibiting the introduction of foreign Lotteries in the Danish Westindia Possessions. The Council then proceeded the preliminary to discussion of the draft of the Municipal Ordinance.

The first Member for Frederikstcd Heilbutli J could not consider the draft worthy of recommendation, nor could he sec that the functions ot the Burgher Councils wero extended by it ; lie was therefore of the opinion, that as long nothing as far superior was offered, it would be most proper I to retain what was in force. He proposed the appointment of a Committee of 5 members. The first Member for Christiansted Arnesen requested the Governor to favor him with an explanation of a passage in 17 of the Draft. þÿ The Burgher Council is entitled to take into consideration every subject regarding the interest of the Municipality, and to make proposals regarding the same, to the superior þÿauthority; to ) which request the Governor responded : that it had not been the intention of the Government to restrict the sphere of action of the Burgher Councils The first Member for St. Johns (llanschell) expressed his great satisfaction with regard to the draft in toto, but he thought it inadvisable that the principle according to which the deficiencies ot the respective Land Treasuries were to be covered by assessment, (which though mentioned and acknowledged in the older Westindia Grdinances, had however never been put in force in consequence of, that at that period the Absentee Tax yielded a considerable revenue) should now be adopted in this draft at a time, when the Land Treasuries are in great distress. Gn account of the paramount importance of the matter, he proposed the appointment of a

Committee of not less than 7 members. In refutation of those objections the Governor observed, that the point in question was not that of a regular, dependant Tax, but merely one that exceptionally could be resorted to, in order to cover a deficiency that might possibly arise. The first Member for Frederikstcd (Ilcilbuth) agreed to the proposal of the appointment of a Committee of 7 members, to which were elected, Messrs. Newton with 14 þÿ Ilcilbuth with 14, þÿ Riisc with 14, þÿ Stenersen with 14, þÿ llanschell with 13, þÿ Arnesen with 12, þÿ Christmas with 9 votes. The preliminary discussions on the draft regarding the Marriages of the Country Laborers were then introduced. The first Member for Frederiksted (Heilbuth) started the question, whether the draft related only to those cases where laborers had been marby post of packages and letters. He observed i ried before concluding the contract of labor, or if it likewise included those marriages solemnized in the course of the year. The first Crown Member (Hawley) stated : that while the regulations relative to this matter were on the one, this draft was on the other extreme, which would lead to the result, that all the marriages of the country laborers would be solemnized in the course of the month of October, wherefore a modification was highly desirable in such a manner, that the law would embrace all marriages entered into at the period when the contracts of labor were closed, thus that in the course of the year, the husband should not be

allowed to quit the Estate where he was domi cilcd, but that the wife should be entitled to move to him. The second Member for Frederiksted Newton J objected to this interpretation, and proposed the appointment of a Committee of 5 members. The first Member for said district Ilcilbuth particularly pointed out, that marriages among the country laborers were by these most frequently considered as a welcome means of expressing their dissatisfaction with the persons in authority on the estate, and that generally speaking some egotistical motive was the cause of their entering into marriage. The Governor declared : that it had been the intention of the Government, that tfic draft should

embrace both cases mentioned by the first member for Frederiksted Heilbuth. The first Member for Christiansted , Arnesen observed : that the benevolent intention, which was had in view in framing the respective provision in the regulations had been eluded by a very strange interpretation, and objected to the appointment of a Committee, which was seconded by the first member for St. Johns llanschell J . At the voting on this subject the appointment of a Committee was rejected by a majority of 10 votes against 7 ; in consequence whereof the draft will be immediately referred to the first discussion.
