Kcipoiittihlc Government and Mell-Reliance. a want of self reliance has hitherto been the bane of the people of Jamaica. Whether it arises from constitutional indolence, or ia the result of the peculiar circumstances in which we have been placed, we will not nmv consider, but it must be patent to every observant individual that there is a sad lack of energy amongst ns. and that the spirit of enterprise has yet to he breathed into the inert mass of society in this island. Wc have been accustomed to look for help anywhere, and everywhere, hut in ourselves. We are little better than overgrown children, requiring the constant supervision and assistance of a nurse. þÿ The child stumbles and falls, but instead of raising himself up, there he will lie blubbering and hollowing, till the friendly hand of "nurse," or "mania," helps him upon his legs again. þÿ Behold here a picture of the Jamaicans. We fall into distress and poverty, hut the thought never enters our minds of helping ourselves out of the slough, anil of regaining our former position. No, we only cry, and cry, and cry till the " mother country" þÿ our kind and indulgent " mama." old England, stretches out her arm, and extricates us from our difficulties. Latterly, however, our tender parent lias been growing wiser, and more resolute, than mi days of yore. Nome say she lias been growing unfeeling of late towards her dear children in this dependency, and that she does not seem to care much whether tliev prosper or not, whether they ale strong or weak, poor or rich, miserable

"f happy. We strongly suspect, however, that her seeming indifference has been caused, not by the growth oi intelligence, and the increase of I rue wisdom. She has found out that the surest way to keep people n a state of þÿchildhood to prevent the developement of Iheir powers þÿ to cramp their energies, and to make them weak, puny, and worthless, is to be always helping them ; ami that, on the other hand the way to ensure their steady and gradual progress towards a healthy and vigorous manhood, is to teach them how to exercise their capabilities, and to keep themselves. It has, therefore, become her settled policy, to render us just so much further assistance only as is compatible with this þÿprinciple as will enable us to set ourselves right. Ai l we think every reflecting man who has the real v "lfare of this country at heart, will applatld her resoaon, and will heartily rejoice that the leading strings Ave been cast off, and our destinies, in a great, measure, placed in our own hands. It la in this light, that we would view the recent propose! > and align;, tions of the British Government to

3 © 1ft 1> at A?!tS« the Jamaica House of Assembly. Under the guise of retrenchment, the ruling party in that House has been agitating for the last seven years, for the restoration of protection. þÿ The commencement of this agitation synchronizes exactly with the passing of the Sugar Duties Bill of 1846, þÿ its cessation and death with the period when the British people, having fully tested the capabilities, and reaped the benefits of free trade, ratified as with a consentaneous voice, the commercial policy of the last seven years, and when our planters saw and felt that their hopes were gone for ever. Those are ignorant of the real character and principles of these gentlemen who imagine that they would remain permanently quiet, if there were the slightest grounds upon which they could build up an expectation of the recovery of that darling and profitable monopoly which they so long enjoyed. Let the hope of protection be hut again awakened in the breast of the planters, and Sir Henry Barklv, free-trader as he is, would find himself in troubled waters, and hotli his wisdom and patience severely tested by the very men who are now as tame arid tractable as iambs, þÿ for the very good reason that they set; they can gain nothing by the manifestation of a contrary spirit. But the question is settled. þÿ The British Government will not, indeed cannot, restore protection either to the corn-growers of England or to the sugar-planters of Jamaica. And the latter must now, like the former, depend upon

their own energy, skill, and industry, for success. Still the Government desires to give us every advantage which is in its power to aft'ord, so that the inevitable change, which has taken place in its commercial policy, might hear upon us as lightly as possible. Hence the offer of a loan, based upon the condition of our reforming our institutions, and establishing a stricter and more efficient supervision and control over t ho public finances of the colony than has hitherto been obtained. Hence the important measure styled "Responsible Government," the manifest purpose and tendency of which is to invest tiie executive with larger powers than he lias ever yet enjoyed, with respect to the collection and disbursement of the public money. But it is a false notion, þÿ and one likely to prove most injurious to our interests, should it obtain the ascendancy in men's minds þÿ that these measures are, of themselves, to ensure the salvation of the þÿcountry to extricate us out of our distracted and suffering island, a golden reign of prosperity and wealth. þÿ And it is just because we are afraid that this idea will obtain a fatal predominancy, and blast the fair hopes which begin to present themselves, that we would lift up the warning voice, and shew our countrymen wherein' their true strength lies, and the course which it would he wisdom in them to pursue Let it be remembered that responsible government, and the proffered loan of half a million, are auxiliary measures, and no more,

designed to assist ns in extricating ourselves by vigorous, determined, and persevering efforts on our part, from present difficulties, and to ensure us a prosperous future. These measures cannot of themselves prove a panacea for the numerous ills under which we are now labouring. They must be supplemented by the steady and well directed exertions of the people of Jamaica. They will then, no doubt, meet the highest expectations of all parties, and not otherwise. these measures. We hear of nothing now but " the VVc fear, however, that too much is looked for Iron) loan" and " responsible government." Is anv evil deplored ? We are told that ' responsible government" will correct it. Is any grievance complained of.' We are assured that responsible government will redress it. Is any improvement projected ? We are advised to leave the matter in tho hands of the ministry that is to lie. The loan and responsible government, are, it appears, to accomplish every thing, and þÿ something i>esides. Now, herein we have a genuine and striking manifestation of the old Jamaica spirit, of leaning upon something or somebody þÿ upon anything or anybody, energy, skill, and industry. Our kind mama" having, rather than bestir ourselves and depend upon our own " in a measure, withdrawn her protection, and told us plainly enough that we must now "do" for ourselves, we straightway begin to look about us for some kind being who will supply her place, and save us the trouble of thinking and acting for ourselves. þÿ Most

opportunely "responsible government' comes forward, and we at once throw ourselves in her outstretched arms, anil reposing there, would fain hope soon to fail into a state of blissful obliviousness oj all our past troubles and sufferings. But let it lie kept in mind, let it be seriously pondered bv all. that nothing can raise us and save us, unless we resolve to help ourselves. The measures to which we have adverted in this article, will, no doubt, do much towards setting mutters right in Jamaica, hut we repeat if, thev will not þÿ they cannot accomplish every tiling. We call upon our countrymen then, throughout the lengtli and breadth of the land, manfullv to put their shoulders to the wheel. It is upon our own exertions, anil upon the blessing of Heaven, that we must now depend for prosperity and happiness.. Let ns then display the spirit, and act the part of men, and not of children, and then Heaven, that denies nothing to the industrious, will crown our efforts with success and " fill our laps with plenty." Let each man, in his sphere, and according to his means and abilities, iiowevf.r limited and humble tiif.y may be, put forth his best exertions to bring about a better state of things, and we shall soon see brighter and happier days in Jamaica. þÿ Watchman.

The Council (hen proceeded to the preliminary discussions relative to medical attendance on estates. The 5tb Member for Christiansted Birch explained those reasons, why he couid not agree to the draft, which is based on the recommendation of the Colonial Council in the year 1852 He directed the Council's attention to the following : first : that the draft is founded on different principles with respect to the 3 islands, thus at the island of St. John the appointment of a public physician is proposed, whose services the planters shall be bound to use, while at St 1 homas and St. Croix it is left to their option to choose what physician they please ; þÿ secondly : that the þÿreasons that called forth the Colonial Council's proposal in 1852 in regard of St. Croix, that it was important that the physician should not be engaged by the laborers but by the planters, in order that be should not be dependent of the former in issuing certificates respecting their state of health þÿ are rejectable, on account of, that the physician, if called upon to give certificates for tho settlement of disputes between owners of estates and the laborers, ought to be independent of both parties ; furthermore : that the right which the draft gives the planter to doduet the payment to the physician out of the wages or not, is in opposition to the existing rules concerning fixed wages : and lastly : that the draft does not provide for medical attendance to the stock estates, which as regards St. Thomas

may soon become of greater importance than the sugar estates, besides wbioh at St. Croix these ostates have sometimes a numerous population ; add to which the enforcing of the draft would meet with many obstacles. He'suggested to the deliberation of the Council, if it might not bo thought preferable, to authorize the Burgher Council to divide the estates in tho island into a certain number of districts, in such a manner that each may be conveniently attended to by the physicians in the island, and to cause the owners of landed property to pay monthly or quarterly into the Landtreasury such an amount, as may be considered sufficient to be fixed for medical attendance on oach individual on the estates, either with or without deduotion out of the laborers' wages, and then to let the Burgher Council ongage a physician for each district, and out of tho contributions davolvmg t.o the Landtreasury, to pay his salary quarterly By adopting this system the aboveststed objections would not bo applicable, and all the country districts in general would bo provided with medical attendance, whioh cannot be obtained by tho draft. Finally he called the attention of the Council to the Chancery's letter of 13th July 1841, the principles of which render it a duty incumbent on the physicians to accept the medical attendance in a country difitriot for a suitable remuneration, in oases where the public demands it.

The first Member for Christiansted ( Arnesen) could not conceive the necessity of any law relative to this case, as it was not called for by any particularly pressing circumstances. Tho first Member for Frederiksted (Heilbuth) pointed out the continually increasing want of medical practitioners in general in this island, and the difficulty for any new physician to obtain a sufficient remuneration for his services. The Couucil agreed to appoint a Committee, to which were appointed, Messrs. Arnesen with 15, " Hanschell with 13, " Heilbuth with 12, " Birch with 10, u Newton with 10 votes. In consequence of a proposal of the first and sixth Members for St. Thomas (Stenersen and Riise) the draft of law relative to several Taxes to the Laud Treasury of St. Thomas was referred to a Committee of 5 members, to which were elected. From the St. George's Chronicle, May 6. THE FRENCH ISLANDS Our intelligence has been scant this fortnignt from Martinique and Guadaloupe. At the former island, the attention of the Government was much occupied with the subject of the currency ; and a monetary reform has been announced which promises beneficial results ment gazette says þÿ to the public. An official announcement in the govern- þÿ in the daily increasing scarcity of silver, felt oven in the mother-country, where silver money has in its turn become the object of a premium or over-valuation, as was previously the case with gold, it is necessary, in the interest of the colony, that efficacious measures be taken to check the efflux of our silver coins and the influx of over-valued gold coins. For several months no business at the Treasury has

been transacted in money bearing an over valuation, and the American Eagle has been rejected altogether from the chests both at Guadaloupe and Martinique. The Spanish doubloon alone, on winch a value of 86 f. 40c. has been fixed by ordinance since 1827, is permitted to be taken at the þÿTreasury. Captain Blanc has contracted with the Colonial Government to import 10,000 Coolies into Martinique in four years, or 2,500 a-year. The captain engages to build two clipper screw-steamers, capable of carrying 1000 Coolies, and of accomplishing the passage from India to Martinique in 50 days. A line of steamers is to be run this vear between Newfoundland and the French Islands, bringing codfish. Her þÿMajesty ship Calypso, having on board His Excellency Lieut.-General Wood, Military Commander-in-Chief of the Windward and Leeward Islands, touched at Martinique on the 8th ultimo on her way from St. Lucia to Dominica. The English General was handsomely entertained during his stay there by the Count de Gueydon. The Calypso touched also at Guadaloupe. þÿ Her þÿsailors, says þÿl Avenir, þÿ strolled along the streets of Point-a-Pitre. to the high gratification of the inhabitants, who manifested a good deal of curiosity to see them ; they are a set of fine hale young fellows with jolly faces and intelligent manners. Some of them went to the guardhouse in the market place, and instantly gave their hands to our brave soldiers in tiie blunt manner of their country, and, such already is the influence of the union of the two nations,

that they fraternized like old friends meeting after a long absence, and the friendly feeling was ratified amid some bottles of beer. It affords us pleasure to say that the behaviour, the politeness and quietness of these sailors, were admired by every body. As for the officers, it is well known how distinguished they are in their deportment and in their courtesy towards Frenchþÿmen. The following Proclamation, on the subject of the War in the East, appears officially in the papers bcfore us : þÿ proclamation : þÿ Inhabitants of Martinique. þÿ The generous efforts of France and England, closely united, have not been able to preserve the peace of the world. þÿ War has broken out. The Emperor has made known to the Senate and to the Legislative Body, that Russia has placed itself in a state of hostilities towards us. Our distance from the theatre of the war renders improbably any attaok of the Russians against this colony, j þÿ Yet be ye prepared for any event. þÿ I rely, with all faith j upon the patriotism of the Inhabitants of Martinique and upon their devotedness to the person of the Emperor. Vive þÿl Empereur ! Comte de Gueydon, Governor, &c., &.C. Fort-de-France, April 21, 1854. A despatch from the Minister of the Marine and Colonies, dated 30th April, reminds the Governor of the opening of the Paris Exhibition of Industry and Agriculture appointed for the 1st of May instant, and suggests the appointment of a Commission, composed of an equal number of such public functionaries and of

other inhabitants as may be able to correspond upon the subject of specimens in botany, mineralogy, &c. to be sent from Martinique. Of the St. Pierre Market, we read in the Outrf.- Mf.r (April þÿ29) Sugar continues abundant, but transactions have not increased on that account. It is with difficulty that good qualities are disposed of at 23f., and common sorts are calm at 18 to 22f. There has been a slight reduction in freight for Havre ; it is at 115 for that port, 125 for Marseilles, and 110 for Bordeaux and Nantes. Tafia (common rum) has corns down, it is no longer sold at more than 40f. per hectolitre. Wc have 21 ships in port, but the greater part of them will be away by the 15th May; fortunately they will be to some extent replaced by vessels now on their way þÿout. þÿ » OOO þÿ Rhiht of Neutrals. þÿ It may he observed that, although the concessions made by our government are of the highest importance, and, indeed, leave nothing to he complained of by the neutral states, their effect on the present war may he less extensive than would seem at first to he the case. All the ports of Russia, in the Baltic, the Black Sea, and the White Sea, can he blockaded effectually, and we have no doubt that it is the intention of the allied powers to render this blockade complete as soon as the season arrives at which the navigation would otherwise he open. At present even the port of Revel is completely blocked up by ice, and the British frigate Miranda, which was sent to reconnoitre
last week, was at one moment so locked in that she was compelled to fire some of her heavy guns to break up the ftoes of ice collected round her. þÿ Times.

Havana, April 27, 1854 His Excellency, the Governor and Captain- General, has, with the date of to-day, been pleased to direct to the Charge þÿd Affaires of Her Majesty in Washington, Mexico, and Venezuela, and to Her þÿMajesty Consuls s in Jamaica and St. Thomas, the following circular : 1 Her Majesty the Queen, our Lady, with date ot 22d March, has been pleased to issue the following þÿ My heart, ever inclined to clemency, has not decree : been able to deny oblivion to the faults of those of my subjects, who erring one day through sorrowful errors and dangerous passions, attempted against the security of my dominions in the Antilles, and against the peace and public order of the island of Cuba ; and taking into consideration the motives mentioned by my council of \ ministers, I decree þÿ Firstly : I conclude a general amnesty to all i those who, for having taking part, directly or indirectly, in conspiracies, rebellions, or foreign in- | vasions, with the intent of causing disturbances, or of committing any other kind of political of- fence in the island of Cuba, who were prosecuted | j ons, or exptilsed by government from their domi- and condemned, being absent from my domini- j ciles. j Secondly : This amnesty does not apply to ! \ those absent, having committed a common crime. Thirdly : Those in prison in Spain, <3fC. , shall j be set free. Fourthly : Those pardoned may reside in Spain j and abroad. 1 Fifthly: Ultamarine Governors, 4c., shall extend the amnesty to those whom it compre-

hends, giving information to the Supreme Government, i(-c. Sixthly : The Governors, 4"0- hall remit notes of the names of the persons admitted to the amnesty, with name of place to which they have ! gone. Havana, ire þÿPEZUELA. We shall look with some interest to the report of Lieutenant St.John, who has now arrived in England ; as also to that of Mr. Gisborne and his assistants. Until we have these it is unfair to pronounce an opinion, but we have u - þÿt that thirty-six lives have been lost in this recent attempt, namely, four of the cr<.w of II M. S. Virago, under the orders of Commander Prerost ; Twenty-two of the party under Lieutenant Strain, U. S. N., and ten New Grenadian soldiers þÿ all of which loss of life will have to be accounted for, and has arisen from a want of proper concert In the first place, it was highly imprudent of the British Rear-Admiral More sby to order Commander Prevost to cross the Tsthmus without the concert of Mr. Gisborne, who was seeking to eonciliate the Indians; by this four British sailors have been sacrificed. In the next place the United States, Captain Hollins, would not wait until the French and British parties arrived, because they would have all the credit of first crossing the isthmus, and in consequence of this precipitancy 22 lives are lost Mr. St. John will explain how the New Grenadian soldiers wero lost. Dr. Cullen reiused to go when requested, and it is the general belief that he has never crossed, and that the whole affair will prove to be very discreditable to all concerned. The Panama Railway is progressing rapidly to completion ; there are at present up-

wards of three thousand men at work on the line. (Concluded ) $ 17. 1 , It is a duty incumbent on all Danish vessels, at the request of the post-department, to j convey the royal mails from tbe starting-place to the harbor for which they are cleared. Such request being made, either in a special instance, or by public advertisement, to vessels in I general, the master of the vessel shall in proper time report to the post-office the day and the hour he intends to start. With regard to voyages between the mother-country and the Danish West India Possessions such report shall be made at least 7 days and with reg ;rd to the passage between the Islands, at least 6 hours, previous to the departure of the vessel, unless it is proved to the post-office that peculiar circumstances compel the vessel to leave prematurely. The cus- ' according to their nature, it is considered tomhouse-department shall co-operate with the post department to the effect that the above mentioned report is made, and that the vessel does not leave before the time fixed, unless the mail is carried on board, accompanied by two similar notes of parcels of which the one shall be return- I

ed to the post-department supplied with the receipt of the master of the vessel, who keeps the other for himself. For the information of the custom house-departmeut at the place of arrival, it shall be entered in the clearance that the vessel carries the royal mail, and the post-office of the place shall give a receipt on the note of parcels, lor the de Pivery of the mail, which receipt shall be produ ced on eiftering the vessel at the customhouse In the Danish West India possessions the mastef hf the ve-st 1 shall, as hitherto, report himself to the post-office mill' an hour before sailing, and receive the letter-mails. It is a duty incumbent on the master of the vessel, during the passage to keep the mail, confided to his care, in the safest and best guarded place in the vessel, especially to put the light (letter) mail in his own cabin and in ease of any accident to take particular care of it. In case the master of the vessel should be compelled to seek another harbor, than the one to which lie is bound, he shall report at the postoffice of the place þÿ or in want of one þÿ to the customhouse-department, that he has the mail onboard ; it shall then according to circumstances be decided whether the mail is to be conveyed further in another way or not. If it is in a foreign country, he shall report himself to the nearest Danish Consulate that shall cause the needful to be done with regard to the further conveyance of the mail. On arriving at the place of destination, the

master us sood as the vessel has come to anchor, shall immediately deliver the light (letter) mail at the post-office and the rest of the mail as soon as circumstances will allow. 2, Sailing vessels and steamers intending to run as packets from an harbor within the post district, shall in proper time at the latest, simultaneously with the first public advertisement thereof, make a report to the post-administration, as well of their route in general, as of the places where they intend to stop, of the hours of starting and arrival, and of all such changes that subsequently may take place in the original arrangement; they shall be bound to receive, and in accordance with the above regulations, to keep and deliver the royal mails at the different stopping places. The post-department has a right at a convenient and accessible place in the vessel, to' place locked boxes, for deposit of letters ; these boxes, together with the mail, to he exchanged at the different stopping-places 18 The obligation resting on Danish vessels, according to the regulation of the 1st of November 1781 7, viz: without any remuneration to convey the West India mail, between the mothercountry and the Danish West India Islands, and between the Islands, shall remain unchanged. To foreign masters of vessels conveying the West India light (letter) mail, or carrying letters to the Danish West India Possessions shall be paid 1 Cent pr. I,oth of the combined Weight of the letters to or from places in America, and the

double amount of letters to or from any other part of the world. This rule is however not applicable if the mail or letters are carried for a foreign post-administration or if otherwise fixed by conventions. Danish vessels conveying West India letters to or from foreign places are to be paid at the same rate. Letters despatched in the letter boxes, mentioned sub 17 No. 2, are not included herein, unless they are supplied with post-stan ps. For all parcels, pertaining to the heavy (package) mail, shall be paid to the owner or the master of the vessel concerned, the weight or volume postage for the sca-transpnrt on the articles transmitted, applied to the total weight or volume of the same. $ 10 All special regulations that arc considered necessary or advisable with regard to post-transmissions, shall he made by the administration of the post-department viz: for the transmission between the mother-country and the Danish West India Possessions, by the administration in the mother-country and for the post-department iD the Danish West India Possessions, by the Colonial Government. It is probable tnal tins curious labyrinth of isle-en- i tangled and coast-sheltered waters, will, after all, be the theatre of our first military operations in the struggle which it is now universally admitted is at hand. We purpose, therefore, presenting our readers with a i sketch of the Baltic and the principal points of interest and importance which are contained within the vast xtent of this inla.nd sea. Its great length and comparatively small breadth, give it the form of an extensive gulf, and such it would be considered if it were not separated from the North Sea by the low and narrow tract of land which forms the southern part of the Danish peninsula called Schleswig. The longest straight line drawn through the Baltic would be about 400 miies, and the width no.vhere exceeds 160 miles. The area is computed at 160,000 .square miles. The þÿh ulf of Bothnia, which is a vast sea in itself, running up between Norway and Finland, joins it on the north, md the Gull of Finland prolongs it in the east. The entrance from the Atlantic is by a large ritlf called the Ka'mgal, which separates Denmark from Norway and | Sweden, and liv three straits, the Sound, the Great Beit and the lettle Beit, which may he considered the three gates by which the Baltic is entered. Having ' passed the pine crowned clitfs of Norway, and threaded the numerous small isles of the Kattegat, we approach these formidable gates. No far as regards the powortul naval expedition that recently left our shores, we

need only consider two of these gates or entrances. Pile southernmost, or l.ittle Belt, which separates the peninsula of Jutland from the island of Funen, is too long, the navigation too intricate, and the depth of water too variable to be attempted bv large vessels. Its whole length is about 80 miles, and in some places, as at I redina, near the entrance, and at Middlefahrt, it is less than a mile in width. The depth varies from lour to 27 fathoms. The middle entrance, the Great Belt, separates the islands of Funen and Zealand. It miles in width. I he navigation of this eight is about 70 miles in length, and from passage is also to twelve dangerous, owing to numerous shoals and small, low islands. The third entrance, the Sound, through which one of the vessels of our fleet passed a few days since, separates Sweden from the island of Zealand. It is about 30 miles long, and at the entrance, where it is narrowest, between Kronburg and llelsinborg, it is only a mile and a halt across. The navigation of this channel is safe, and the depth of water varies from 10 to 20 fathoms. The fortress of Kronborg, which is about 26 miles from Copenhagen, is placed at the ex-

0 4 D 'll AT 2 3« tremity of the tongue of land on which stands the town and castle of Elsinour, and commands the entrance of the Sound. The whole of these three entrances are strongly fortified, and are as completely the keys of the Baltic, as the castles and fortresses of the Dardanelles are the keys of the Black Sea and Constantinople; and it is somewhat singular that nature has thus interposed obstacles to the ambitious designs of Russia, by placing her, as it were, under arrest in her own vast dominions, with sentries at her only points of egress both in the north and the south. Within the Baltic. þÿ Having passed the Sound, and arrived at Copenhagen, we are fairly within the Baltic. The northern shores are generally high and j precipitous, and covered with magnificent pine forests, producing timber of the finest quality; the southern coasts, on the contrary, are low and marshy, and lined by numerous sand banks all the way to the entrance of the Gulf of Finland. The basin of the Baltic is of considerable extent, and it receives tiie waters of several large rivers, and the drainage of more than a fifth of the surface of Europe. Perhaps in no other inhabited country on the face of the globe does so much snow fall in the course of the year as in the countries round the Baltic. This phenomenon may be accounted for by the atmosphere of the sea being filled alternately with warm moisture, and subject to a dry piercing cold, and by the rapid transition from one to the other. The provinces bordering the Baltic are the richest granary

of the globe ; and no portion of the earth approaching so near to the polar circle can he compared to them in natural wealth. The immense quantity of melted snow water that tails into the Baltic renders it much less salt than the Black Sea. Its average depth is small compared with its area, being only forty to sixty fathoms. It is to these two circumstances, its comparative freshness and want of depth, is to be attributed that the shores, and nearly the whole of its surface, are every year covered with ice, which in general, from the end ol December to the beginning of April locks up completely the harbours, straits, and bays, and interrupts the navigation. In severe winters large portions of the Baltic have been frozen sufficiently hard to allow of an army to cross. The current is not rapid ; it sets outward towards the Kattegat, and the tides are scarcely felt, the rise or fall at Copenhagen scarcely exceeding a foot. Another peculiarity of the Baltic, and ol the gulfs i.i which it terminates, is exceedingly important as regards the naval expedition which lias just entered its wafers. The ice does not leave the whole of tliis vast sheet simultaneously. The western parts are free and disengaged much sooner than the eastern, and from west to east the process of liberation once begun, stretches further and further by wellknown gradations. Probable Naval Operations. þÿ It must he borne in mint! that the Russian fleet is not concentrated in any one place, and if it were possible (which is for Sir

Charles þÿNapier j s udgment, and not for any layman) safely to enter the nearer waters the moment they are free, and to follow the thaw as it advances, it is evident that the Russian ships found successively in various ports, or intercepted in their egress, or overtaken in their flight, must fall in detail, easy, and almost bloodless prizes, without a blow. The attempt would have its hazards, and those most accustomed to the navigation and to fhe localities might tarn the best. It is well known that many a good vessel has perished just alter the thaw, amid rocks and obstacles that no chart can indicate, viz., the huge rolling masses of half sunken ice, which, for many days, encumber the whole of that expanse from shore to shore. With regard to these waters, it may be remarked that the equipment of our expedition bears an immediate and most satisfactory relation to their peculiarities. There never yet was a fleet so completely furnished with the formidable agencies of stelm þÿ and steam in its most efficient form of warlike application þÿ steam with the screw propeller, the motive machinery of which is considerably below the waterline, and out of the range of the þÿenemy t s iro. On the other hand there is no sea in Europe where there might he more pressing occasion for steam to facilitate the warlike operations of a fleet. In the Black Sea, where there are sudden and violent storms, steam might often save a vessel, and, | indeed, this new power must be an advantage every-

where ; but in the Baltic, which is almost wholly formed hy the concentric discharge of great rivers, and where very little wind power, nr opportunity from ocean currents, can ever be anticipated, the moment ( for an operation might, without the resources of steam, pass away before the ships could he concentrated at the required spot. ____ - þÿKJS--

Opening oe Japan. þÿ The visit of Commodore Perry July in last has, doubt, hastened the no event whieh his return would probably have accomplished ; hut the actual achievement is due to the Russians, not to the Americans. While Commodore Perry deemed it the wisest course, after delivering the letter of the President of the United States in due form, at Urga, to allow six months to elapse before requiring an answer, Admiral Pontiatine, without dictating the place where he should hold intercourse with the Japanese authorities, went, as directed, to Nangasaki, and has succeeded in negotiating, apparently without any sacrifice of national dignity, and with the sort of success which- the world was more prepared to expect from the practical republic

than from the Russian Autocracy. According to the information we have received from an authentic source, some time after the Russian Ad iniral had intimated his presence and objects at Nangasaki, two high officers arrived, and, after entertaining him at a least on shore, entered upon the objects of the visit in a friendly and even cor- | dial manner. In substance they stated very candidly that the Japanese government seeing the earnest desire of foreign nations to hold intercourse with them, and their own people being anxious to trade, it had been resolved to open the commerce of Japan to all nations. In this spirit all the ports of Japan might at once he considered as open to foreign vessels requiring to refit or to take in supplies of wood and water ; but, to avoid disturbances, the orews must not be allowed to land. This, however, is only confirming whaj foreigners have already enjoyed, without always fairly ackowledging. With regard to commercial intercourse, the Japanese officers stated, that after centuries of seclusion some preparations were necessary, and a year must therefore elapse before any treaty or privilege to trade could come into operation. We have no doubt as to the accuracy ol this information, and are further inclined to believe that a similar result might have been effected long ago by Great Britain, if she had ever been fortunate enough to intrust her interests in this part of the globe to any one who did not look steadily and exclusively to his own for-

tunes, and how to obtain honours without deserving them. Dr. Bowring may not be insensible to either, but he is less likely than any of his predecessors, or any admiral we have seen on the station, to overlook the opportunity of achieving a lasting reputation for himself þÿ China Mai!

TRANSLATION.) Ordinance ronevrning trades and professions in the Danish Wcstindia Possessions.

We Frederik the Seventh, T!y the grace of God King of Denmark, the Vandals and the Goths, Duke of Sleswick, Holsteen, Stormarn, Ditmarsh, Lanonbore and Oldenburg, Make known : On the report of Our Minister of Finance who has laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council on a Draft of an Ordinance concerning trades and professions in the Danish Westindia Possessions, We most graciously decree Chap. I. n The trades and occupations hereafter mentioned . shall generally be exercised only by persons having taken out burgherbriefs corresponding : 1. Trading wholesale or by retail ; also those branches of business mentioned in the 4th J of this ordinance, 2. Mechanica1 trades, if carried on with the aid of assistants and apprentices, 3. Ownership of vessels, if the owner be not a merchant, the business of master or captain of a vessel, of architect, civil engineer, printer, 4. þÿPlanter sbusiness, either as owner of a cane estate with þÿworks provided the party resides in the Island and is otherwise qualified to be a burgher þÿ or as paid administrator or manager thereof. If a special license be required for certain branches of trade, for instance, for keeping a tavern, an apoþÿthecary shop, s a printing office, the parties concerned shall nevertheless take out burgherbriefs. j2. Whoever intends to qualify as a bnrgher for the exercise of any of the said trsdea or professions shall address his petition to that effect to the superior authority of the respective Island ; the petition stating his
age and place of birth to be delivered to the policcmastar, who will forward it after certifying thereon as to

any legal impediment to the grant of a burgherbrief ; the petitioner, particularly if he be a s ranger having resided in the Island only for a short time, shall be called on for sufficient explanations, or attestations of trustworthy inhabitants as to his former living and conduct. Whenever the exercise of the trade intended, under the provisions of this ordinance, depends on a practical proof of skill, the performance thereof must be proved. No person shall be admitted as a burgher before he has completed his 25th year, or has been made of age by license. Burgherbriefs for managers of estates and for masters of vessels may be granted when the party has completed 21 years. Before the issuing of a burgherbrief, the party concerned shall prove payment to the Land-Treasury of the amount fixed by this ordinance, and of one fourth part thereof to the State Treasury ; also, in the Island of St. Croix, the payment of $2 56 for a stamp ; and the oath required of burghers shall be taken in the Seþÿcretary office, s from which the burgherbrief is issued. The burgherbrief shall not be acted on, before it has been exhibited to the policemaster of that jurisdiction, jn which the party intend to settle, and certified by him to have been noted in the proper protocol; for the entry and certificate there shall be paid a fee equal to one eight part of the amount payable to the Land-Treasury. » 3. Excepting the cases mentioned in the 9th $ of this ordinance, the burgherbrief authorises the party con-

cerned to follow the branch of business therein specified only in that Island, for which it has been issued, and of which generally he must be a resident. When circumstances admit of one or several occupations being carried on by the same person in different islands, viz: as administrator of several estates, or as resident merchant in either of the towns and proprietor of an estate in another Island, such party shall take out a burgherbrief in each place. Fora burgherbrief entitling the party to carry on several trades in the same Island shall be paid the full amount of fees and charges only for one trade (if the rates be different, then for the one rated highest) and besides one half of the fees and charges for each of the other trades The same rule is applicable, whenever a burgher desires his burgherbrief to be extended to other trades, or will give up his actual burgherbrief in order to take out a new burgherbrief for some other trade ; in such cases the fees and charges paid previously shall be deducted from the total amount. The widow of a burgher sha'I generally be entitled to continue his business on the strength of his burgherbrief, as lung as she remains unmarried. Chap II. 4. Mercantile business shall only be carried on in the towns, excepting the cases specified in this ordinance. For a burgherbrief entitling the holder to carry on trade both by wholesale and by retail, there shall be charged 860, payable to the respective Land-Treasury ; in St. Thomas with the addition of one third of that

amount. For a burgherbrief as retailer the charge shall be 836, payable to the respective Land Treasury ; in St. Thomas with the above addition. When several persons are trading in partnership each of the partners shall take out a burgherbrief. Apothecaries shall take out burgherbriefs as retailers, unless they intend to carry on trade by wholesale with other merchandise than authorized by their licenses as apothecaries, in which case they shall take out burgherbriefs as merchants. A special burgherbrief shall he required for keeping a rumshop or a tavern, to be paid for as a þÿretailer s burgherbrief ; the same for butchers killing horned cattle for selling. 5. Licenses to carry on selling by retail without burgherbriefs may on petition be granted by the government of the respective Island to unmarried females above 25 years of age, and to widows; such petition to be reported on and forwarded by the respective policemasters. For such licenses there shall be paid to the Landtreasnry 818, in St. Thomas with the addition of one third thereof, and further a payment to the State Treasury and a police-fee in the proportion fixed by k 2. The Government may likewise grant licenses to carry on petty trade as hucksters to unmarried females above 25 years of age, to widows and to males, without burgherbriefs; for every such licence there shall be paid to the Landtreasury 12, in St. Thomas with the addition stated above, besides a proportionate payment to the State-Treasury and police-fee.

From the Morning Herald, March 4, 1851. The following circular, dated the 23rd ult., has been sent by M. Ducos, Minister of Marine, to all the superior officers of the navy, with instructions relative to their conduct in the present crisis : þÿ þÿ Monsieur, þÿ My dispatch of the 18th of this month has called your attention, in a special manner, to the grave complications which the Eastern question has produced in Europe. The negociations entered into for the purpose of settling pacifically the difference which has arisen between Russia and Turkey have remained without result, and everything leads to the supposition that new efforts will remain ineffective. England and France have resolved to protect the Ottoman empire, and to oppose, even by force, the projects of encroachment of Russia. These two great nations arc intimately united in their policy, and have reciprocally given each other the most certain pledges of their alliance. Their squadrons aro cruising together in the Black Sea, and they give to each other the most sincere cooperation. The two governments, after having adopted a common policy, have also come to an understanding respecting all the means of action. This alliance of France and England is to make itself known not merely in the seas of Europe. The government of his Imperial Majesty and that of the Queen of Great Britain desire to have the same union and the same accord prevailing in every latitude of the world. Inconsequence, the naval forces of England and France are bound to afford each other a mutual co-operation in every

country, even the most distant. Immediately after the receipt of these instructions, you must take care to placo yourself in relation with the commanders of stations and captains of vessels belonging to Great Britain ; and you will which in concert with them, all the measures combine, may have for object to protect the interests, the power, or tbo honour of the flag of the two united nations. To that end, you aro to lend each other a mutual assistance, whether for attacking the enemy when hostilities shall have commenced, or when the declaration of war shall have been made, or for defending yourselves if necessary. You aro to accord your protection to all trading-vessels of Great Britain in the same way as the vessels of war of Eng' and will afford aid and protection to our trading-vessels. In a word, the two governments of Franco and England desire that their naval forces shall act as if they belonged to ono and tbo samo nation. I reckon on your never losing sight of this rule of conduct, and on always acting on it in such a manner as to cement more and more, if possible, the intimate union of

the two countries. As long as hostilities between France and England on the ono hand and Russia on the other shall not have commenced, or that the declaration of war shall not have been made, you will avoid taking the initiative in measures of aggression, and you will remain on the defensive. I will take care, when the proper moment shall have come, to transmit to you the necessary instructions for attacking. Receive the assurance of my highest consideration. þÿ Theodore þÿDucos.

HOUSE OF LORDS. The Earl of Ellenbcrvugh said The true point of this country to lock to was the Baltic, net the Black Sea. If we could only_ establish our superiority to Russia in the Baltic then we must be safe. How could her Majesty's ministers say that in the course of the next three weeks our fleet may not be required in the Baltic ? How could they tell whether Sweden may not feel obliged to call upon them for assistance ? Sweden and Denmark were both increasing their military force, and why ? Because they laboured under the apprehension of being attacked by Russia. It was quite possible, then, that we may at no distant period be called upon to go to their defence upon their own shores. If such should be the case, how fatal must the consequences be of having dispatched so large a force to assist Turkey in the East. But it was not only in support of Sweden and Denmark that our troops might bo tinguished required. It was quite possible that that deem officer Sir Charles Napier might disit essential to our success in the contest against Russia that our forces should occupy one ot those islands in the Baltic which was now occupied by Russia. Nothing was more probable than that such might be the case, and yet our forces had been seut off to Turkey. The more he thought upon the subject, the more did he feel convinced that 20,000 men at our disposal for the Baltio would have more effect in obstructing the designs of Russia, and in weakening her powers of resistance, than any number of men which it might

be in our power to seud to the Black Sea. In the Baltic it was the great blow must be struck in the establishing the superiority of our arms there þÿ impending contest. If we could only succeed in if we could take the Russian islands in that sea, and destroy the Russian arsenals before the troops at Cronstadt could have overcome the obstacles thrown in their way by the ice, then we should have struck a blow which must place the triumph of our arms beyond all possibility of doubt. Of this lie felt quite sure, that if by pursuing the course to which he had just been referring, wo should have obtained the advantage, as we must, of detaining the troops of Russia upon the shores of the Baltic, instead of permitting her to send them for service elsewhere, the influence of such a state of things upon public opinion in Denmark, in Sweden, and even in St Petcrsburgh itself, would be far more advantageous to us than anything which was likely to result from the dispatch of 20,000 men to Constantinople (hear, hear.)

Religious Toleration in Sweden. þÿ It is known that in Sweden conversion from the Protestant (Lutheran) religion is strictly forbidden. The public prosecutor of Stockholm has just commenced a prosecution before the criminal court of that city of six married women, named Funk, Offermann, Schytz, Anderson, Wallander, and Muller, and of an unmarried one, named Lundogren, for having abandoned the Lutheran faith, in which they were baptised, and embraced that of the Roman Catholic church. He demands that, according þÿ demned to be exiled from the kingdom of Swe- to the criminal code, they shall bo conden, and to be deprived of the right of inheritance, and of all civil þÿrights.

At the burial of a married woman, in Dublin, on Monday, the gravediggers, while filling in the earth, heard sounds issue from the coffin ; it was quickly dug out and uncovered, when the body was found quite warm ; the physician gave it as his opinion that the poor woman could not have been dead more than an hour, being the period that had elapsed when the sounds were first heard.
